title: Search index
short: Map each word to the documents that contain it.
what: Finding 'red shoes' by reading every product is far too slow at millions of items. A search index (an inverted index) is built ahead of time: for each word, a list of the documents that contain it. A search jumps to those lists and combines them.
analogy: The index at the back of a book. Look up 'volcano' and it says pages 12, 48 and 203, so you never read the whole book.

frames.label: products
frames.say: Four products. Reading each one to find a word works for 4, not for 50 million. So build an index ahead of time.

frames.label: index: word -> doc ids
frames.say: Split doc 1, 'red shoes', into words. Under each word, write the doc id: red -> 1, shoes -> 1.

frames.label: index: word -> doc ids
frames.say: Doc 2, 'blue shoes', adds 2 to the shoes list and starts a new word, blue.

frames.label: index: word -> doc ids
frames.say: After docs 3 and 4 it's done. Words point to docs, the reverse of docs holding words, so it's called an inverted index.

frames.label: search 'red shoes'
frames.say: Search 'red shoes': jump straight to 2 rows. red -> 1, 3 and shoes -> 1, 2. No product text is read.

frames.label: search 'red shoes'
frames.say: Keep the ids that are in both lists: doc 1. Then rank the hits, for example by how rare each matched word is.

when: Rank results by how well they match
cost: Find the docs for one word
O(a + b), the two list sizes
watch: Clean words the same way when indexing and searching: lowercase, strip punctuation, 'running' -> 'run'.
Very common words (the, a) have huge lists: skip them or treat them specially.
The index is a copy that lags a second or so behind; the database stays the source of truth.
interview: Design product search for an online store
